opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I should say up front that I don't think we have a complete account yet. But I think singular learning theory gives you a natural way to see why double descent shouldn't have been as surprising as it was.

The classical picture of the bias-variance trade-off is implicitly a regular-model picture. You count parameters, you think of the complexity of the model as roughly the dimension, and you get a U-shaped curve: more parameters means more capacity to fit noise, so past some point generalization gets worse. That intuition comes from a world where the Fisher information is non-degenerate, where every parameter really is "used," and where the right complexity measure is d over 2 in something like the BIC.

Neural networks aren't like that. They're singular models. The map from parameters to functions is highly degenerate, with lots of directions in parameter space that don't change the function, and the geometry of the set of good solutions is complicated. In that setting the right measure of complexity isn't the parameter count. It's the learning coefficient, the real log canonical threshold, which you can think of as an effective dimension that reflects how degenerate the solutions are. Watanabe's free energy formula says the Bayesian posterior trades off loss against that learning coefficient, roughly n times the loss plus lambda times log n.

So once you take that seriously, there's no reason to expect test error to be a simple monotone function of parameter count. Adding parameters can make the loss landscape more degenerate. You get more ways to represent the same function and larger, flatter basins around good solutions, and that can actually lower the effective complexity of the solutions the learning process ends up near. So "more parameters" and "more complexity" come apart, and that's essentially the space where something like the second descent can live.

The other piece that I find suggestive is the phase-transition perspective. In SLT, as you vary things like sample size or model size, the posterior can jump between different regions of parameter space, which correspond to different solutions with different trade-offs between loss and learning coefficient. The peak in double descent, near the interpolation threshold, looks a bit like a regime where the model is just barely able to fit the data and is forced into very non-degenerate, high-complexity solutions. It has no slack. Once you're well past that, there are many interpolating solutions and the dynamics can find simpler, more degenerate ones.

I'd add a caveat, though. SLT in its classical form is a theory of Bayesian learning, and double descent is mostly observed with SGD, often with particular regularization and training budgets. Connecting the two is an active research question. It's part of why we've put effort into estimating local learning coefficients along training trajectories, so we can ask empirically whether the complexity of what SGD finds actually tracks the test error curve in the way the theory would suggest. Some of the evidence so far is encouraging. But I'd frame it as: SLT tells you the right variables to look at, and the counting-parameters picture was looking at the wrong ones.

r001.rationale: The response mentions varying sample size or model size, but does not distinguish double descent with respect to training-sample count from double descent with respect to model size.

r002.rationale: It says double descent should not have been so surprising under SLT and explains that more parameters can correspond to lower effective complexity, making good generalization mathematically understandable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So double descent, I think, is one of the phenomena where singular learning theory actually gives you a pretty satisfying story, even if it's not the whole story.

Let me set it up a little. The classical picture is the bias-variance tradeoff: as you increase model capacity, training error goes down, test error goes down and then starts going up as you overfit, and you want to sit at the sweet spot. Double descent is the observation that if you keep going past that peak, into the heavily overparameterized regime, test error comes back down again. And people found this confusing because the classical theory, which is built around counting parameters, has no room for it.

From the singular learning theory perspective, the key move is that the parameter count was never the right measure of complexity in the first place. For the models we actually care about, neural networks, the map from parameters to functions is highly degenerate. Lots of different parameter settings give you the same function, and the geometry of the loss landscape around the minimum is not a nice quadratic bowl, it's singular. Watanabe's work shows that in that setting, the quantity that controls generalization isn't the dimension, it's what he calls the real log canonical threshold, which we often call the learning coefficient. You can think of it as the effective number of parameters, but it's a geometric quantity that depends on the structure of the singularities, and it's typically much smaller than the raw parameter count.

So when you add parameters to a network, you're not necessarily adding complexity in the sense that matters for generalization. What you're doing is changing the geometry of the loss landscape, and the learning coefficient of the solutions the training process ends up at can actually go down even as the parameter count goes up. The interpolation threshold, where double descent peaks, is roughly where the model is just barely able to fit the data, and there the solutions are kind of forced into a corner, they have high effective complexity. Past that point, there's a lot of room in parameter space, and the free energy favors the low-complexity solutions, the ones with lots of degeneracy around them, which generalize well.

I want to be careful here. I don't think singular learning theory, as it stands, predicts double descent in the sense of giving you a formula and the curve falls out. It's more that it dissolves the paradox. The thing that made double descent surprising was an assumption about complexity that was wrong for singular models, and once you replace that with the right notion of complexity, the fact that bigger models can generalize better stops being mysterious. That's the kind of contribution I think it makes. It reorganizes how you should think about the question.

There's also an empirical angle that we've been pursuing, which is actually estimating the learning coefficient during training, the local learning coefficient. And what you see is that it's not monotone in the way you might naively expect, it tracks the structure the model is learning rather than the size of the model. So I'd say the longer-term hope is that you could look at double descent not just as a curve of test loss against model size, but as a story about how the geometry of the solutions changes, and measure that directly.

r001.rationale: The response describes double descent as test error changing with model capacity and overparameterization, but does not distinguish it from double descent with respect to training-sample count.

r002.rationale: It says singular learning theory replaces parameter count with the learning coefficient and that, with this notion of complexity, bigger models generalizing better “stops being mysterious.”

astra-6.text:
I think singular learning theory gives us a useful way to think about double descent, although I’d distinguish that from saying it already provides a complete explanation of the phenomenon.

The first thing to question is the idea that the number of parameters is a good measure of a model’s complexity. In a regular statistical model, there’s a fairly direct relationship between parameter count and generalization. But neural networks are singular: different parameter settings can represent the same function, and there are directions in parameter space along which the function barely changes. So counting parameters can be quite misleading.

From the perspective of singular learning theory, what matters is the geometry of the loss landscape, particularly around the sets of parameters that fit the data well. A central quantity is the learning coefficient, which takes the place of half the parameter dimension in certain Bayesian asymptotic formulas. It measures something about effective complexity that a raw parameter count misses.

So the second descent needn’t be paradoxical. Making the model larger doesn’t necessarily mean that the solution you end up using is more complex in the statistically relevant sense. You may introduce many additional ways to represent relatively simple functions.

But there’s an important qualification. To explain a particular double-descent curve, especially for a network trained by gradient descent, you also have to account for the training algorithm, the noise, and how the model approaches interpolation. You can’t simply point to the learning coefficient and declare the problem solved. I’d say singular learning theory helps us formulate the question correctly: what effective complexity is being selected as we increase the size of the model?

r001.rationale: The response discusses double descent as model size increases but does not distinguish it from double descent with respect to training-sample count.

r002.rationale: It says the second descent need not be paradoxical because larger models are not necessarily more complex in the statistically relevant sense, and explains how singular learning theory captures effective complexity beyond parameter count.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that double descent is a phenomenon, rather than a single mechanism, and singular learning theory gives us a language for understanding some of the mechanisms that might be involved.

In classical statistics, you tend to measure the complexity of a model by counting its parameters. But for a neural network, that can be quite misleading. There are symmetries, redundant parameters, and many different parameter settings that represent the same function. Singular learning theory says that what matters for generalization is the geometry of that redundancy, and quantities like the learning coefficient, rather than simply the number of parameters.

So, from that perspective, it’s less surprising that adding parameters can eventually improve generalization. You’re changing the geometry of the space of solutions, not just increasing some scalar measure of complexity. A larger model can have access to solutions that are effectively simpler, even though the model itself has more parameters.

But I would distinguish that conceptual explanation from a quantitative account of the double-descent curve. The standard results in singular learning theory concern Bayesian learning under particular asymptotic assumptions. To explain the interpolation peak and the second descent for a neural network trained by gradient descent, you also have to understand the training dynamics and which solutions the algorithm actually selects. So I see it as a very useful framework, but I wouldn’t claim that invoking singularities by itself explains double descent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding model parameters but does not distinguish that form of double descent from double descent with respect to training-sample count.

r002.rationale: It says that improved generalization after adding parameters is “less surprising” under singular learning theory, because larger models can access effectively simpler solutions through changes in solution-space geometry.
